title: Time & space complexity
overview: Before learning data structures you need a way to say how fast a program is and how much memory it uses. This module teaches Big-O notation by counting how many times loops run: constant, logarithmic, square-root, linear, n log n and quadratic. Every later module uses this language to compare solutions.

concepts.explain: Big-O describes how the work grows when the input size `n` grows. We keep only the fastest-growing term and drop constant factors, so `2n + 5` becomes O(n).
A loop that moves its counter by a fixed step (`i++`, `i += 2`) up to something like `n`, `n/2` or `2n` runs a number of times proportional to `n`, so it is O(n).
concepts.snippet: for(int i = 0; i < 2*n; i++)  // still O(n)

concepts.explain: When the counter is multiplied or divided each round (`i *= 2`, `i /= 3`), it reaches `n` in about log n steps. Doubling from 1 reaches 1,000,000 in only 20 steps.
concepts.snippet: for(int i = 1; i <= n; i *= 2)  // O(log n)

concepts.explain: Divisors come in pairs `i` and `n/i`, and one of each pair is at most sqrt(n). So stopping at `i*i <= n` finds all divisors in O(sqrt n).
Loops inside loops multiply: n outer rounds times n inner rounds is O(n^2); an inner log loop gives O(n log n); an inner loop to `m` gives O(n*m).
Loops placed one after another add up. O(n) + O(n) is still O(n); O(n^2) + O(n log n) is O(n^2) because the biggest term wins.
Space counts the extra memory the program asks for. A few variables are O(1), an array of size `n` is O(n), an `n x n` grid is O(n^2).
Sometimes maths removes a loop completely: the sum 1+2+...+n equals `n*(n+1)/2`, which is O(1).

files.title: Sum 1..n with a formula
files.what: Reads a number and prints the sum from 1 to that number. The loop version is commented out and replaced with the formula `n*(n+1)/2`, turning O(n) work into O(1).
steps: Print a prompt and read `num`.
The commented loop would add 1, 2, ..., `num` one by one: `num` steps.
Instead compute `sum = (num * (num + 1)) / 2` in one step.
Print the result in a sentence.
files.output_note: The prompt `Enter a number: ` and the answer appear on the same line because the input you type is not echoed: for 10 you see `Sum of numbers from 1 to 10 is 55` (10*11/2 = 55).
files.watch_out: `num * (num + 1)` overflows `int` once `num` passes about 46,000. Use `long long` for big inputs.

check.q: Why is the formula version O(1) while the loop version is O(n)?
check.a: The formula does the same three arithmetic operations no matter how big `num` is; the loop runs once per number from 1 to `num`.

files.title: Linear loops, O(n)
files.what: Five different loops that each run a number of times proportional to `n`: up to `n`, `n-5`, `n/2`, `2n`, and `n` with step 2. All are O(n) because constants are dropped.
steps: Read `n`.
Loop 1 prints `0..n-1`: exactly `n` rounds.
Loop 2 stops at `n-5` and loop 3 at `n/2`: fewer rounds, but still a fixed fraction of `n`.
Loop 4 goes to `2*n`: twice as many rounds, still O(n).
Loop 5 goes to `n` in steps of 2: about `n/2` rounds.
Adding five O(n) parts gives O(5n), which we write as O(n).
files.output_note: All numbers come on one line. For n = 8, split them into the five loops: `0..7` (8 values), `0 1 2` (8-5 = 3), `0 1 2 3` (8/2 = 4), `0..15` (16 values), then `0 2 4 6 8`.

check.q: A loop runs `i` from 0 while `i < 3*n + 100`. What is its Big-O?
check.a: O(n): drop the constant factor 3 and the added 100.

files.title: Logarithmic loops, O(log n)
files.what: Four loops whose counter grows or shrinks by multiplying or dividing, so they finish in about log n rounds.
steps: Loop 1 doubles `i` from 1 while `i <= n`: 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
Loop 2 starts at `n` and divides by 3 while `i >= 1`: log base 3 of n rounds.
Loop 3 prints `i`, then does `i *= 2` inside the body and `i++` in the header, so `i` becomes `2i+1` each round: still roughly doubling.
Loop 4 does the same with `k = 3`, so `i` becomes `3i+1` each round: log base 3.
The base of the log does not matter in Big-O, so all four are O(log n).
files.output_note: For n = 20 the single line splits into four groups: `1 2 4 8 16` (doubling), `20 6 2` (dividing by 3), `1 3 7 15` (i -> 2i+1), `1 4 13` (i -> 3i+1). Each group is tiny compared to 20.
files.watch_out: Loops 3 and 4 change `i` both in the body and in the header; trace them by hand once so the jump pattern does not surprise you.

check.q: About how many times does `for(i = 1; i <= n; i *= 2)` run when n = 1,000,000?

files.title: Square-root loops and divisors
files.what: Shows loops that stop at sqrt(n) and uses the idea to list all divisors of `n` in O(sqrt n) instead of O(n).
steps: Loop 1 simply counts `i` from 0 up to `sqrt(n)`.
Loop 2 is the slow divisor finder: test every `i` from 1 to `n` with `n % i == 0` (O(n)).
Loop 3 only tests `i` up to `sqrt(n)`; when `i` divides `n`, it prints both `i` and its partner `n / i`.
Loop 4 does the same but writes the stop condition as `i*i <= n`, which avoids floating-point `sqrt` entirely.
files.complexity: Time O(sqrt n) for the fast loops, O(n) for the plain divisor loop · Space O(1)
files.output_note: The program does not compile, so there is no output. If it did, for 36 the fast loops would print pairs `1 36 2 18 3 12 4 9 6 6`.
files.watch_out: Compile error: `sqrt` is used without `#include <cmath>`. Add that include to fix it. Also note that for a perfect square like 36 the pair `6 6` prints 6 twice; add `if (i != n/i)` before printing the partner to avoid the duplicate.

check.q: Why is it enough to test divisors only up to sqrt(n)?
check.a: Divisors pair up as `i` and `n/i`, and the smaller one of every pair is at most sqrt(n), so each pair is found from its small side.

files.title: Nested loops: O(n^2), O(n*m), O(n^3)
files.what: Nested loops multiply their round counts. Two loops to `n` give n^2, a loop to `n` around a loop to `m` gives n*m, and three loops give n^3.
steps: Read `n` and `m`.
Block 1 prints every pair `i j` with both below `n`: n*n lines.
Block 2 prints `Hello` n*n times.
Block 3 prints `Hello` n*m times (the inner loop goes to `m`).
Block 4 has three nested loops: n*n*n lines.
The whole program is O(n^3 + n*m); the biggest term decides.
files.output_note: With n = 2, m = 3: first 4 lines of pairs (`0 0` to `1 1`), then 18 `Hello` lines = 4 (block 2) + 6 (block 3, 2*3) + 8 (block 4, 2*2*2).

check.q: If n doubles, how much longer does an O(n^2) loop take?

files.title: O(n log n) vs O(n^2)
files.what: Compares a normal nested loop (O(n^2)) with a nested loop whose inner counter doubles (O(n log n)).
steps: Block 1: outer `i` to `n`, inner `j` to `n`, so n*n lines.
Block 2: outer `i` to `n`, inner `j` starts at 1 and doubles while `j < n`, so about log n rounds per outer round.
Total for block 2 is n * log n, which grows much slower than n^2.
Sorting algorithms like merge sort have this O(n log n) shape.
files.complexity: Time O(n^2) overall (block 2 alone is O(n log n)) · Space O(1)
files.output_note: Each line is `iHelloj`. For n = 3, block 1 prints 9 lines (`0Hello0` .. `2Hello2`); block 2 prints 6 lines where `j` only takes values 1 and 2 (doubling from 1 stops before 3).

check.q: For n = 1024, roughly how many lines does block 2 print compared to block 1?
check.a: Block 2 about 1024 * 10 = 10,240 lines; block 1 about 1024 * 1024 = 1,048,576 lines.

files.title: Space complexity examples
files.what: Notes about memory: single variables are O(1), a 1-D array of size `n` is O(n), an `n x n` array is O(n^2), and an `n x m` array is O(n*m). Time depends on loops; space depends on what you allocate.
steps: `sum`, `x`, `d` are single variables: O(1) space each.
The loop adding `i` into `sum` takes O(n) time but no extra memory.
`int a[n]` reserves `n` ints: O(n) space; reading it takes O(n) time.
`int a[n][n]` reserves n*n ints: O(n^2) space, even though the loop only fills the diagonal in O(n) time.
`int a[n][m]` reserves n*m ints: O(n*m) space.
files.complexity: Space up to O(n^2) · Time O(n)
files.input_note: n, then n numbers (if the program compiled).
files.output_note: The file is a set of notes and does not compile, so there is no output. Read it for the comments on space.
files.watch_out: Compile errors: `m` is never declared, and the name `a` is declared three times (`a[n]`, `a[n][n]`, `a[n][m]`). Fix by declaring `int n, m;` and giving the arrays different names (`a`, `b`, `c`).

check.q: A loop runs n times but only updates one variable. What are its time and space complexities?

recap: Count how many times the loop body runs; drop constants and smaller terms.
Counter +1 or +k: O(n). Counter *2 or /2: O(log n). Stop at i*i <= n: O(sqrt n).
Nested loops multiply, loops in sequence add.
Order from best to worst: O(1) < O(log n) < O(sqrt n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n).
Space complexity counts allocated memory: variables O(1), array O(n), grid O(n^2).
A maths formula can replace a whole loop (sum 1..n = n(n+1)/2).

check_yourself.q: What is the complexity of `for(i=n; i>0; i/=2) for(j=0; j<n; j++)`?
check_yourself.a: O(n log n): the outer loop runs about log n times and the inner loop runs n times each.

check_yourself.q: Is O(2n + n^2) the same as O(n^2)?
check_yourself.a: Yes. The n^2 term dominates, and the 2n term is dropped.

check_yourself.q: Roughly how many simple operations per second should you assume, and what does that mean for n = 10^5?
check_yourself.a: About 10^8 per second, so O(n^2) = 10^10 is too slow while O(n log n) (about 1.7 * 10^6) is fine.

body: You have written a lot of loops by now, and each one was either right or wrong. From here on a program can be right and still fail: the judge stops it after 1 second, and a correct answer that arrives too late scores nothing. So you need a way to say how much work a program does, before you run it.
The way is to count steps. Take a loop you wrote in your first weeks, the one that adds the numbers from 1 to `n`:
The line `sum += i` runs once for each value of `i`, so it runs `n` times. That is the whole measurement: how many times does the body run? Now watch what happens as the input grows.

Double `n` and the work doubles. The count follows `n` in a straight line, and that shape has a name: **O(n)**, said "order n". The `O` says we only care about the shape of the growth, not the exact number, so a loop that runs `2n + 5` times is still O(n) - doubling `n` still doubles the work.
Now a second shape. To check whether an array of `n` numbers holds two equal values you compared every pair, a loop inside a loop:
The inner body now runs about `n * n` times. That is **O(n^2)**, and the difference is not small:
**What is new here.** Until now you judged a program by the answer it printed. From this module on you also judge it by how its step count grows when the input grows.
A third shape appears when the counter is multiplied instead of increased. Start `i` at 1 and double it each round:

Twenty steps for a million. Multiplying or dividing the counter each round gives **O(log n)**, and the count hardly moves when `n` grows: a billion needs about 30 steps. Dividing works the same way, which is why `i /= 3` is also O(log n).

One more you will meet: a loop that stops at `i*i <= n` runs about sqrt(n) times, 1000 steps for a million. Divisors come in pairs, `i` and `n/i`, and one of each pair is at most sqrt(n), so that short loop still finds them all.
intro.snippet: for(int i = 1; i <= n; i *= 2) cout << i << " ";

body: **Why the shapes matter.** A rough rule: a computer does about 10^8 simple steps in one second. Put the shapes next to that limit.

For `n` = 100000 an O(n) or O(n log n) solution finishes comfortably, while O(n^2) needs about 10^10 steps and has no chance in 1 second. That single comparison decides which idea you write down, and it is why every later module argues about solutions in this language.

**Memory tells the same story.** A few variables are O(1) space, an array of `n` numbers is O(n), an `n` by `n` grid is O(n^2), which is why a 100000 by 100000 grid cannot exist. And sometimes the count collapses to nothing: 1 + 2 + ... + n equals `n * (n + 1) / 2`, one multiplication and one division whatever `n` is, so O(1).
The programs below go shape by shape: linear loops, logarithmic loops, the square-root loop, nested loops, O(n log n) against O(n^2), and space.
